claims.claim_text: Wallach reports that doctors are strikingly short-lived for people who advise everyone else on health. An 1895 edition of the Journal of the American Medical Association put the average life of a doctor at just 55 years, and when Wallach checked whether that gap had closed a century later, he found it had narrowed by only three years. By his figures doctors today still average only about 58 years, far short of the roughly 75.5 years the average American reaches — the founding observation behind 'Dead Doctors Don't Lie.'
claims.verbatim:
what he discovered, in an 1895 edition of the Journal of the American
Medical Association was that the average life of doctors was just 55 years. Anticipating this gap to
be much closer today than 100 years ago, he researched it further. What he found was that today, the
gap is closer-but only by three years.

claims.claim_text: Premature gray, white, or silver hair is, in Wallach's reading, the first visible sign of copper deficiency — because copper is the cofactor the body needs to manufacture hair pigment. He backs it with a favorite story: a flock of turkeys dying of ruptured aortic aneurysms whose deaths stopped once copper was doubled in the feed, since copper also builds the strong elastic fibers in artery walls. Other copper-shortage signs he lists include skin wrinkles, spider and varicose veins, and an iron-resistant anemia.
claims.verbatim:
Copper deficiency in human beings presents itself first as white, gray, or
silver hair.

claims.claim_text: It was discovered in turkeys during the 1950s. When turkeys were switched to a new 'complete' feed-pellet ration, fully half of them died within the first thirteen weeks, and autopsies showed almost all had died of a ruptured aortic aneurysm. A pathologist reasoned it had to be copper deficiency, because copper is required to manufacture the heavy elastic fibers in artery walls — and when the copper in the feed was doubled the next year, not a single turkey died of a ruptured aneurysm.
claims.verbatim:
In the first thirteen weeks on the original
complete pellet ration, fully half of the turkeys on this ration died. Farmers
were picking them up by the bushel baskets full and taking them to the state
diagnostic lab to see what they died from.
At autopsy, it was obvious that almost all of the dead turkeys had died from
a ruptured aortic aneurysm. One clever pathologist said, “This has got to be
due to a copper deficiency, because copper is required to manufacture the
heavy elastic fibers found in arteries.” The next year the amount of copper
was doubled in the feed pellets and not a single turkey died from a ruptured
aneurysm.

claims.claim_text: Wallach reads the common 'liver spots' or 'age spots' on older skin as an early outward sign of selenium deficiency — and warns they are only the visible tip. When someone shows ten age spots on the skin, he says, they carry millions of the same deposits throughout the brain, eyes, heart, liver, and other organs. This 'pigment of aging,' known scientifically as ceroid lipofuscin, is essentially accumulated rancid fat (free radicals) that clogs cell function and, in his view, sharply raises the risk of cancer, Alzheimer's disease, and heart disease.
claims.verbatim:
Another early symptom of selenium deficiency in older humans is the
appearance of “liver spots” or “age spots.”

claims.claim_text: Yes. Wallach says selenium was universally thought to be toxic until 1957, when it was found to be an essential trace nutrient. Selenium deficiency causes a whole family of diseases — infertility, miscarriages, cystic fibrosis of the pancreas, animal Sudden Infant Death Syndrome, liver cirrhosis, stiff lamb disease, white muscle disease, muscular dystrophy, anemias, encephalomalacia (which he equates with Alzheimer's disease), cardiomyopathy, and mulberry heart disease. In each case, selenium supplementation prevented the disease and in many cases reversed or cured it — the livestock industry does this for a few pennies a day.
claims.verbatim:
For example, the mineral selenium was universally thought to be toxic until
1957 when it was found to be an essential nutrient in trace amounts in
laboratory animals and livestock. Selenium deficiency causes infertility,
miscarriages, cystic fibrosis of the pancreas, Sudden Infant Death
Syndrome in animals, liver cirrhosis, stiff lamb disease, white muscle
disease, muscular dystrophy, anemias, encephalomalacia (Alzheimer’s
disease), cardiomyopathy heart disease, and mulberry heart disease. In each
case, selenium supplementation prevented the disease and in many cases
reversed or cured existing diseases, which were all significant causes of
animal losses to the livestock industry.

claims.claim_text: Zoo marmosets and shrews died of diabetes attributed to chromium and vanadium deficiency (observed at autopsy).
claims.verbatim:
I saw marmosets, alligators, and
shrews that died of diabetes, a chromium and vanadium deficiency.

claims.claim_text: Calcium deficiency alone can result in as many as 147 different diseases (osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, Bell's palsy, tinnitus, trigeminal neuralgia, spinal stenosis, and more).
claims.verbatim:
Calcium deficiency alone could result in as many as 147 different diseases
ranging from osteoporosis, osteoarthritis, osteomalacia, degenerative
arthritis, Bell’s Palsy, tinnitus, trigeminal neuralgia, and spinal stenosis to
name a few.

claims.claim_text: Wallach describes trace-mineral deficiency as a cascade that ends in what he calls the 'clinical phase' — the point where the body can no longer compensate and full-blown disease sets in, including cardiomyopathy, diabetes, cancer, and liver cirrhosis, and even death. His pointed twist: these clinical deficiencies are almost never diagnosed as mineral shortages by conventional doctors, yet the 'cure' is often simply replacing the missing element, with positive responses sometimes appearing in as little as 48 hours to 30 days.
claims.verbatim:
The clinical phase of trace mineral deficiencies is characterized by the onset
of full-blown disease states and even death—i.e., cardiomyopathy, diabetes,
cancer, liver cirrhosis.

claims.claim_text: The recommended maintenance dose for germanium is 20–30 mg per day (50–100 mg/day is used for serious illness requiring increased oxygenation).
claims.verbatim:
Twenty to 30 mg per day is the recommended maintenance dose for
germanium. Fifty to 100 mg per day doses are commonly used when an
individual has a serious illness that requires an increased oxygen level in
the body.

claims.claim_text: Wallach treats silver as an essential trace mineral with a germ-killing role. Humans can take about 400 micrograms of silver a day, he says, and a silver deficiency results in an impaired immune system. He describes silver as an antibacterial, antiviral, and antifungal agent that works by disabling the enzymes microorganisms use to breathe — the same property that once led people to drop a silver dollar into milk to keep it from spoiling. He cites Dr. Robert Becker's The Body Electric linking low tissue silver both to more illness and to poor tissue repair.
claims.verbatim:
Humans can
consume 400 mcg of silver per day. A silver “deficiency” results in an
impaired immune system.

claims.claim_text: Silver's power against germs comes down to a specific mechanism, Wallach explains: it acts as an antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal 'anti-metabolite' that disables the very enzymes microorganisms rely on for respiration — in effect, it suffocates them. He notes this is why silver sulfadiazine is still used in most American burn centers to prevent infection, and why silver was dropped into milk and onto wounds long before modern antibiotics existed.
claims.verbatim:
Silver is an anti-bacterial, anti-viral, anti-fungal, anti-metabolite that
disables specific enzymes that microorganisms use for respiration.

claims.claim_text: Per USDA researcher Richard Anderson, 90 percent of Americans are deficient in chromium.
claims.verbatim:
According to Richard Anderson, USDA, “Ninety percent of
all Americans are deficient in chromium.”

claims.claim_text: Yes. Wallach cites work by Gary Evans of Bemidji State University, Minnesota, which clearly showed a 33.3 percent increase in the lifespan of laboratory animals supplemented with chromium. He frames it as a landmark: before this study, gerontologists led by Roy Walford believed a severe restriction of calories was the only way to extend life past the expected average — Evans showed that a single trace mineral could do it.
claims.verbatim:
Gary Evans, Bemidji State University, Minnesota, very clearly showed an
increased life span in laboratory animals by 33.3 percent when they were
supplemented with chromium. Prior to this study gerontologists, led by Roy
Walford, felt a severe restriction of calories was the only way to extend life
past the expected average.

claims.claim_text: Chromium deficiency produces a wide range of clinical diseases (low blood sugar, type II diabetes, elevated triglycerides/cholesterol, coronary vessel disease, infertility) and a shortened lifespan, aggravated by concurrent vanadium deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiencies of chromium in humans are
characterized by a wide variety of clinical diseases as well as a shortened
life expectancy. The clinical diseases of chromium deficiency are
aggravated by concurrent vanadium deficiencies.

claims.claim_text: Cesium chloride is used in alternative cancer therapy ('high-pH therapy'), entering the cancer cell to produce an alkaline environment.
claims.verbatim:
Cesium chloride is used as part of alternative cancer therapy programs.
Cesium provides “high ph therapy” for cancer by entering the cancer cell
and producing an alkaline environment.

claims.claim_text: Pica (a compulsion to eat ice, dirt, or lead paint) is a specific sign of iron deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Experimental evidence shows very clearly that “pica” is a specific sign of
iron deficiency. Pica can drive children and adults to eat ice (pagophagia),
dirt (geophagia), or lead paint.

claims.claim_text: Iron absorption is governed by the gut environment: stomach hydrochloric acid is required for optimal absorption of iron, and ascorbic acid (vitamin C) increases it, while clays and phytates decrease it. Wallach adds that impaired absorption from high-fiber, high-phytate diets makes the standard 18 mg RDA too low for people eating that way.

Yes. Excess iron can cause cirrhosis of the liver, fibrosis of the pancreas, diabetes, and heart failure. Wallach's key point is the mechanism: these diseases are not the direct toxic effects of iron itself, but the result of the excess iron raising the body's needs for selenium, copper, zinc, and other nutrients — so the harm is really a driven deficiency of those minerals.
claims.verbatim:
Excesses of iron can cause cirrhosis of the liver, fibrosis of the pancreas,
diabetes, and heart failure. These diseases are not the direct toxic affects of
iron, but rather the increased iron results in the increased needs of selenium,
copper, zinc, etc.

claims.claim_text: Iodine's whole reason for being essential, Wallach explains, is that the body combines it with the amino acid tyrosine to manufacture thyroxin, the main thyroid hormone that sets the body's metabolic rate. He warns iodine intake is usually low to begin with, and that Americans cutting back on salt at their doctors' urging have pushed goiter and hypothyroidism toward epidemic levels — all the more since iodine is freely lost in sweat.
claims.verbatim:
In combination with the amino acid tyrosine,
iodine is manufactured into the thyroid hormone thyroxin.

claims.claim_text: Since Americans began restricting salt intake on doctors' advice, goiter and hypothyroidism have become epidemic (iodized salt was a key iodine source).
claims.verbatim:
Iodine intake is
usually low to begin with, but since Americans have begun restricting their
salt intake at the advice of their doctors, goiter and hypothyroidism has
become epidemic.

claims.claim_text: Copper is a required cofactor to utilize iodine; copper deficiency can drive an iodine-deficiency (goiter) state even where soil iodine is adequate.
claims.verbatim:
A severe copper deficiency
in the soils of the north and the south cause the deficiency state because
copper is a required cofactor to utilize iodine.

claims.claim_text: Manganese deficiency causes birth defects (congenital ataxia, deafness), asthma, convulsions, skeletal defects, and joint problems including temporomandibular joint (jaw) disorder, repetitive motion syndrome, and carpal tunnel syndrome.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiency diseases of Mn are very striking, ranging from severe birth
defects (congenital ataxia, deafness, chondrodystrophy), asthma,
convulsions, retarded growth, skeletal defects, disruption of fat and
carbohydrate metabolism to joint problems in children and adults (i.e. TMJ,
Repetitive Motion Syndrome, Carpal Tunnel Syndrome).

claims.claim_text: Manganese is an essential mineral with both an enzymatic and a structural role. Wallach notes it activates numerous enzyme systems — including those for glucose metabolism, energy production and the antioxidant superoxide dismutase — and is a major constituent of the body's metalloenzymes, hormones and proteins. Structurally, he says it is part of both the developmental process and the finished form of the three fragile ear bones (the ossicles) and of joint cartilage.
claims.verbatim:
Manganese is part of the developmental process and the structure
of the three fragile ear bones and joint cartilage.

claims.claim_text: Molybdenum earns its 'essential' status, Wallach explains, by forming an integral part of at least three enzymes the body relies on: xanthine oxidase, aldehyde oxidase, and sulfite oxidase. It is a clear illustration of how a mineral present in only trace amounts can still be indispensable — each of these enzymes depends on its molybdenum atom to do its job at all.
claims.verbatim:
Molybdenum is known to be an integral part of no less
than three essential enzymes: Xanthine oxidase, Aldehyde oxidase, and
Sulfite oxidase.

claims.claim_text: Selenium is the most efficient antioxidant, working in the glutathione peroxidase enzyme system to keep body fats from going rancid.
claims.verbatim:
Selenium is the most efficient antioxidant (anti-peroxidant).
It’s used at the subcellular level in the glutathione peroxidase enzyme
system and metalloamino acids (selenomethionine, etc.).

claims.claim_text: Selenium's job is to keep the fats in your cells from oxidizing; vegetable oils are polyunsaturated fats that oxidize easily — especially once heated or hydrogenated into trans fats. So Wallach's warning is about the combination: flood the body with rancidity-prone oils while selenium (the antioxidant that would protect them) runs low, and the oils go rancid inside your cells, driving free-radical damage. He calls high vegetable-oil intake concurrent with selenium deficiency “the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer,” and ties the same pairing — including too much fish oil — to birth defects, arteriosclerosis, cardiomyopathy, and sudden cardiac death. The practical point: to him these oils aren't just empty calories, they actively consume the protection selenium is meant to provide.
claims.verbatim:
High intakes of vegetable oils,
including salad dressing and cooking oils, concurrent with a selenium
deficiency is the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer. The polyun‐
saturated configuration of the oils when heated or treated with hydrogen
(“trans fatty acids”) literally causes the rancidity (“free radical” damage) of
cellular fat

claims.claim_text: Tin deficiency in rats produced poor growth, hearing loss, and bilateral (male-pattern) hair loss; Wallach links tin to male-pattern baldness and hearing loss.
claims.verbatim:
Rats fed tin at 17.0 ng/gm show poor growth, reduced feeding efficiency,
hearing loss, and bilateral (male pattern) hair loss, while rats fed 1.99
|ng/gm were physiologically and anatomically normal.

claims.claim_text: Strontium deficiency is associated with certain calcium- and boron-resistant forms of osteoporosis and arthritis.
claims.verbatim:
Deficiencies of strontium are associated with certain types of Ca and boron
resistant osteoporosis and arthritis.

claims.claim_text: Strontium is a trace mineral most highly concentrated in mammalian bone. Wallach says it can replace calcium in many organisms, including man, and that there is considerable evidence it is essential in mammals. He associates a strontium deficiency with certain calcium- and boron-resistant forms of osteoporosis and arthritis.
claims.verbatim:
Strontium
can replace calcium in many organisms, including man. There is
considerable evidence for essentiality in mammals including man.
Deficiencies of strontium are associated with certain types of Ca and boron
resistant osteoporosis and arthritis

claims.claim_text: Vanadium appears to function like insulin by altering cell-membrane function for ion transport — making the membrane's insulin receptors more sensitive to insulin, and benefiting people with glucose and carbohydrate intolerance.
claims.verbatim:
Vanadium appears to function
like insulin by altering cell membrane function for ion transport.

claims.claim_text: Yes. Wallach says vanadium (proven essential in 1971) functions like insulin: it stimulates blood-sugar (glucose) oxidation and transport, and in diabetic rats fed vanadium the blood glucose matched normal controls despite low serum insulin. It works by making the cell-membrane insulin receptors more sensitive to insulin, which benefits glucose and carbohydrate intolerance such as hypoglycemia and prediabetes. He states vanadium supplementation could reduce or even eliminate most cases of adult-onset diabetes, and cites a 1985 University of Vancouver statement that 'vanadium will replace insulin for adult onset diabetics.'
claims.verbatim:
Vanadium supplementation can have a major positive
economic impact by reducing or even eliminating most cases of adult onset
diabetes.

claims.claim_text: Wallach reports that vanadium has known anticarcinogenic properties. In mice, feeding 25 micrograms of vanadium per gram of diet blocked the induction of mammary tumor growth; the vanadium supplement reduced tumor incidence, lowered the average tumor count per animal, and prolonged the median cancer-free time — all without inhibiting the animals' overall growth or health.
claims.verbatim:
Vanadium has known
anticarcinogenic properties. Feeding 25 |ng of vanadium per gram of diet
blocked induction of mouse mammary tumor growth.

claims.claim_text: Zinc's importance is easy to underestimate until you count the enzymes that depend on it: at least 70 metalloenzymes require zinc as a working cofactor, Wallach notes — among them carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, and carboxypeptidase, which handle jobs from carbon-dioxide transport to protein digestion. Zinc also sits inside the RNA molecule itself (the 'zinc fingers') and drives DNA synthesis and cell division, which is why a shortage reaches into so many systems at once.
claims.verbatim:
There are no less than 70 metalloenzymes that require Zn as a
functional cofactor.

claims.claim_text: Zinc is central to the cell's genetic machinery. Wallach says it takes part in the metabolism of nucleic acids and the synthesis of proteins, and is an integral part of the RNA molecule itself — providing the 'metallic fingers' that take part in cell division and the synthesis of DNA. He notes that DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and thymidine kinase are both zinc-dependent enzymes.
claims.verbatim:
Zinc participates in the metabolism of nucleic acids and the synthesis of
proteins. Zinc is also an integral part of the RNA molecule itself where Zinc
provides the “metallic fingers” and participates in cell division and
synthesis of DNA. The DNA-dependent RNA polymerase is a zinc-dependent enzyme, as is thymidine kinase

claims.claim_text: Zinc deficiency, in Wallach's account, produces a wide range of diseases — from congenital birth defects present at birth to degenerative diseases across every age group. He ties an exhaustive list of congenital birth defects to zinc shortage during pregnancy: Down's syndrome; cleft lip and cleft palate; brain defects (dorsal herniation, hydroencephalocele); micro- or anophthalmia (small or absent eyes); agnathia (small or absent lower jaw); spina bifida; clubbed limbs; syndactyly (webbed toes and fingers); polydactyly (extra limbs and digits); atresia (failure to develop limbs, digits, organs, or the anal opening); diaphragmatic, hiatal, umbilical, and inguinal hernias; heart defects; lung defects; and urogenital defects (horseshoe or small kidney, and intersex malformations of the genitalia).
claims.verbatim:
Zinc deficiency
produces a wide range of diseases including congenital birth defects and
degenerative diseases of all age groups.
Congenital Birth Defects Associated with Zinc Deficiency
• Down’s Syndrome
• Cleft lip
• Cleft palate
• Brain defects (dorsal herniation, hydroenchalocoel) • Micro or
anopthalmia (small or absent eyes)
• Agnathia (small lower jaw) • Spina bifida • Clubbed limbs
• Syndactyly (webbed toes and fingers) • Polydactyly (extra limbs and
digits) • Atresia (failure to develop limbs, digits,organs, anal opening,etc.)
• Hernias (hiatal, diaphragmatic, umbilical, inguinal, etc.) • Heart defects (
Lung defects
• Urogenital defects (horseshoe kidney, small kidney, intersex
malformations of the male and female genitalia)

claims.claim_text: Getting enough zinc isn't only about how much you eat — Wallach flags what blocks it: an excess of dietary copper or iron, and high-phytate diets (he singles out vegan eating), all reduce the availability of the zinc you take in, because they compete for or bind the mineral in the gut. He notes zinc is also lost heavily in sweat, which puts unsupplemented athletes at particular risk of deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Excesses of dietary copper and iron and high phytate diets (vegans) will
reduce availability of dietary zinc.

claims.claim_text: From his years as a barefoot doctor among the Zulu, Wallach watched textbook nutritional deficiencies play out in children. Vitamin A shortage, he recounts, caused keratitis and corneal ulcers that could progress all the way to blindness — the eye being one of the first tissues to fail without it. He lists it beside the other deficiencies he treated there: calcium (bone disease), iodine and copper (goiter and miscarriage), and folic acid or zinc (spina bifida and cleft palate).
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin A deficiencies in
children caused keratitis, corneal ulcers, and blindness.

claims.claim_text: Wallach says spina bifida and cleft palate are not true 'genetic' defects but the visible fingerprint of a simple nutritional deficiency — chiefly a lack of folic acid and/or zinc (and vitamin B12) in the mother's diet. He produced these very defects in animals by feeding pregnant mothers diets deficient in zinc, B12, and folic acid, and prevented up to 98% of them by supplying the proper nutrients before conception. In infants he attributes spina bifida and serious cleft palates to folic acid or zinc deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
I studied dozens of congenital birth defects in laboratory and farm animals
and what nutritional deficiencies produced them. What we found was that,
in most instances, “genetic defects” are simple mineral deficiencies that
leave a repeatable “fingerprint” on a specific gene, in a specific location, on
a specific chromosome. They are no more complicated in concept than a
deficiency of zinc resulting in a cleft palate or spina bifida in a farm animal

claims.claim_text: Beriberi is the classic thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency disease. Wallach describes it as a common disease of the Asian rice cultures (the name is Sinhalese for 'I cannot'), characterized by weakness in the legs, hands, and arms together with congestive heart failure, with death from pulmonary edema and abdominal 'dropsy.' He identifies the cause as a thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency — historically appearing where the diet was polished white rice with its thiamine-bearing bran removed.
claims.verbatim:
Beriberi with resultant congestive
heart failure was common, the result of a thiamin or vitamin B1 deficiency.

claims.claim_text: Vitamin B12 is a water-soluble red crystalline substance; its red color comes from the cobalt atom at its center.
claims.verbatim:
Vitamin B12 is a red crystalline substance that is water soluble. The red
color is due to the cobalt in the molecule.

claims.claim_text: About 30 percent of vitamin B12's activity is lost during cooking, whether by electric, gas, or microwave heat, according to Wallach. He explains why it is so fragile: B12 is a water-soluble, red crystalline vitamin — its color comes from the cobalt atom at its center — and it is slowly deactivated by acid, alkali, light, and oxidizing or reducing substances, so ordinary heat degrades a meaningful share of it.
claims.verbatim:
About 30 percent of B12 activity is lost during cooking
(electric, gas, or microwave).

claims.claim_text: Yes. Wallach says it has been known since 1958 that supplemental chromium will prevent and treat both diabetes and hypoglycemia, and points to Walter Mertz (director of USDA field services), who published the chromium-diabetes facts in Federation Proceedings. He calls diabetes the ultimate case of a whole medical specialty that could be wiped out by universal chromium supplementation, because in his framework adult-onset diabetes and hypoglycemia are fundamentally deficiencies of chromium and vanadium — so supplying those minerals corrects the root cause.
claims.verbatim:
Since
1958, it has been known that supplemental chromium will prevent and treat
diabetes as well as hypoglycemia. Just ask any health food storeowner or
N.D.! Walter Mertz (the director of the U.S.D.A. field services) published
the facts associated with chromium and diabetes in the Federation
Proceeding. Here is the ultimate case of a whole specialty of medicine
which could be wiped out by universal chromium supplementation

claims.claim_text: Wallach holds that vanadium can act as a substitute for insulin. He reports that despite low serum insulin, diabetic animals fed vanadium held the same blood glucose as normal controls, because vanadium functions like insulin by altering cell membrane function for ion transport. On that basis he argues that vanadium supplementation can reduce or even eliminate most cases of adult-onset (type 2) diabetes, and cites a 1985 statement from the medical school at the University of Vancouver, BC that vanadium will replace insulin for adult onset diabetics.
claims.verbatim:
the medical school at the
University of Vancouver, BC, Canada stated that “vanadium will replace
insulin for adult onset diabetics.”

claims.claim_text: Wallach's diabetes program opens with the two minerals he ties to blood-sugar control — chromium and vanadium — at 250 micrograms a day in the early stages. He adds a caution: introduce them carefully, because as they sharpen the body's own glucose handling, a diabetic still taking the old dose of insulin or pills can be tipped into 'insulin shock,' a sudden, dangerous drop in blood sugar. The answer is to keep testing and taper the medication as levels come down.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of diabetes should include chromium and vanadium at 250
mcg/day in the initial stages to prevent “insulin shock”

claims.claim_text: The diabetes regimen also includes zinc 50 mg three times daily, B-complex 50 mg three times daily (with niacin), EFAs 5 g three times daily, B12 1,000 mcg/day, quercetin 150 mg/day, copper 2-3 mg/day, lecithin 2,500 mg three times daily, and glutathione 100 mg/day.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of diabetes should also include zinc at 50 mg t.i.d., B-complex at
50 mg t.i.d. (be sure to include niacin which is part of the GTF “glucose
tolerance factor”), essential fatty acids at 5 gm t.i.d., B12 at 1,000 mcg/day,
bioflavonoids including quercetin at 150 mg/day, copper at 2-3 mg/day,
lecithin at 2,500 mg t.i.d., and glutathione at 100 mg/day.

claims.claim_text: Osteoarthritis and degenerative arthritis are a complex of nutritional deficiencies; rheumatoid arthritis's overt cause is chronic Mycoplasma infection.
claims.verbatim:
osteoarthritis and degenerative arthritis are a complex of
nutritional deficiencies. In the case of rheumatoid arthritis, a chronic
infection with a Mycoplasma spp. is the overt cause.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's arthritis protocol rebuilds joint tissue nutritionally rather than just masking pain. The core is calcium at 2,000 mg/day (more if you eat meat two or three times a day), magnesium at 800-1,000 mg/day, and cartilage -- collagen, glucosamine sulfate and chondroitin sulfate -- at 1,000 mg three times a day. He adds vitamin C to bowel tolerance, B6 100 mg twice daily, B3 450 mg twice daily, vitamin E 1,000 IU/day, copper 2 mg/day, selenium 300 mcg/day and zinc 50 mg three times daily, favoring plant-derived colloidal minerals (up to 98 percent absorbable). For rheumatoid arthritis he additionally treats the underlying Mycoplasma infection -- low-dose tetracycline or minocycline for a year (or oral food-grade H2O2) plus IV EDTA/H2O2 chelation.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of arthritis should include calcium at 2000 mg/day and more if
you eat meat two or three times per day. Also take magnesium at 800-1000
mg/day, and cartilage (collagen, glucosamine sulfate and
chondroitin sulfate) at 1000 mg t.i.d. For
rheumatoid arthritis, add tetracycline or minocycline at the low dose acne
therapy level daily for one year, or oral food grade H2O2 to deal with the
Mycoplasma infection. IV chelation with EDTA and H2O2 is very helpful!

time-release capsules. Take Vitamin E at 1000 IU/day. Copper at 2 mg/day
(may be absorbed from a copper bracelet), selenium 300 mcg/day, zinc 50
mg t.i.d. Plant derived colloidal minerals are 98 percent absorbable and give

claims.claim_text: Yes -- Wallach reframes many named 'diseases' as malabsorption in disguise. He argues that celiac-type damage to the intestinal lining (from wheat gluten, cow's-milk albumen or soy protein) can destroy up to 85-90 percent of the absorptive surface, so the body starves for minerals even on an adequate diet. On that basis he calls celiac disease the basic cause of many diseases, including diabetes (malabsorption of chromium and vanadium), cancer (malabsorption of zinc, vitamin A and selenium), and muscular dystrophy / cystic fibrosis (malabsorption of selenium). He describes asthma the same way -- a disease of malabsorption with deficiencies of essential fatty acids, manganese and magnesium -- and atopic dermatitis as a malabsorption syndrome.
claims.verbatim:
Asthma is a
disease of malabsorption with essential fatty acid deficiencies and
deficiencies of manganese and magnesium.

claims.claim_text: Cor pulmonale treatment includes resolving the lung disease plus oxygen, intravenous (into a vein) hydrogen peroxide, and selenium at 500-1,000 mcg/day for adults.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of cor pulmonale includes resolving the precipitating lung
disease and oxygen, IV hydrogen peroxide, and selenium at 500-1,000 mcg
per day for adults.

claims.claim_text: Wallach treats cradle cap (seborrheic dermatitis of infants) by loosening the greasy scale and correcting the deficiencies underneath it. His protocol is regular shampooing to loosen the greasy crust, vitamin B6 at 10-25 mg/day, and zinc at 15-25 mg/day, plus a pulse test for food allergies, which can contribute to the problem. Because he classes cradle cap as a seborrheic dermatitis that can arise from celiac-type intestinal lesions and a malabsorption syndrome, he also supports it with biotin (100 mcg three times daily), folic acid, more B6, vitamin E, essential fatty acids and vitamin A.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of cradle cap includes shampooing regularly to loosen the greasy
scale, B6 at 10-25 mg per day, and zinc at 15-25 mg per day. Food allergies
can contribute to this problem—do a pulse test.

claims.claim_text: Cancer prevention includes beta-carotene at ~300,000 International Units/day (vitamin A equivalent) and selenium at 250-500 mcg/day, alongside a low-fat, high-fiber, fried-food-free diet.
claims.verbatim:
Try to OD on beta-carotene
(almost impossible—first sign is dry skin) at about a vitamin A equivalent
of 300,000 IU per day. Use selenium at 250 to 500 mcg per day.

claims.claim_text: Per the US government, the five-year cancer survival rate has not changed in 20 years despite new surgery/radiation/chemotherapy — untreated patients as a group survived longer.
claims.verbatim:
CHEMOTHERAPY—IN FACT, UNTREATED
PATIENTS, AS A GROUP, SURVIVED LONGER!

claims.claim_text: Osteoporosis is easy to prevent and cure, Wallach claims from personal experience, with two unglamorous things: stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) and calcium. His logic is that the real problem is often not too little calcium in the diet but too little stomach acid to absorb it — so supplementing HCl unlocks the calcium a person already eats. He dismisses the conventional estrogen-and-fluoride approach as failing to touch that root absorption problem.
claims.verbatim:
In our personal experience
osteoporosis is easy to prevent and cure with proper supplementation of
stomach acid (HCl) and calcium.

claims.claim_text: Yes -- Wallach says osteoporosis is easy to prevent and cure. He argues the orthodox push for estrogen and fluoride supplementation does not solve it, because the real problem is failure to absorb and supply calcium. In his experience it prevents and reverses with proper supplementation of stomach acid (HCl) and calcium: betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes 75-200 mg three times daily before meals, plus calcium and magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg/day (or more for the first 30 days), with plant-derived colloidal minerals supplying calcium, magnesium and boron. He also recommends a pulse test for the food allergies that cause celiac-type malabsorption.
claims.verbatim:
The big push by the “orthodox”
doctors is for estrogen and fluoride supplementation, yet these two
compounds alone do not solve the problem. In our personal experience
osteoporosis is easy to prevent and cure with proper supplementation of
stomach acid (HCl) and calcium.

claims.claim_text: Osteoporosis treatment includes betaine hydrochloride and pancreatic enzymes (75-200 mg three times daily before meals) plus calcium and magnesium at 2,000 and 1,000 mg/day or more for the first 30 days.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of osteoporosis should include betaine HCl and pancreatic
enzymes at 75-200 mg t.i.d. 15 minutes before meals, and calcium and
magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day or more for the first 30 days.

claims.claim_text: Wallach considers estrogen the wrong treatment for osteoporosis, and a risky one: it may be contraindicated because of a carcinogenic effect — it is known to cause breast and uterine cancer. His deeper objection is that he does not see osteoporosis as an estrogen-deficiency disease at all, but as a mineral-and-absorption failure — his program corrects stomach acid with betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes and supplies calcium, magnesium and the plant-derived colloidal minerals (including boron) that bone actually needs. In that view hormone replacement treats a symptom while missing the real deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
Estrogen may be contraindicated because of the potential carcinogenic
effect: it is known to cause breast and uterine cancer.

claims.claim_text: Wallach makes a striking claim about earaches: in reality, he says, 95 percent of all otitis (inflammation of the ear) is the result of a milk allergy rather than a primary infection. Instead of the conventional route of antibiotics and surgically inserted ear tubes, he urges a pulse test to confirm the food trigger, strict avoidance of cow's milk in every form, and local relief with hydrogen-peroxide or mullein eardrops alongside the baseline nutritional program. Left uncorrected, he warns, a milk allergy can drive high fever, severe earaches, and even burst eardrums.
claims.verbatim: In reality, 95 percent of all otitis (earaches) is the result of a milk allergy.

claims.claim_text: The essential fatty acids are linoleic, linolenic, and arachidonic acids; 3% of total daily calorie intake should come from EFAs (linoleic and linolenic are strictly essential).
claims.verbatim:
Three polyunsaturated fatty acids (linoleic, linolenic, and arachidonic acids)
are known as essential fatty acids (EFA). Three percent of the total daily
calorie intake is required from EFA.

claims.claim_text: Essential fatty acids matter most where growth is fastest, and Wallach flags their deficiency in infants specifically: it results in poor growth, eczema, and lowered resistance to infectious disease. He frames these good fats as far more than fuel — they lower serum cholesterol and are the raw material for prostaglandins, the local hormones that help regulate blood pressure, heart rate, blood-vessel and airway width, clotting, and brain and spinal-cord function.
claims.verbatim:
EFA deficiency in human infants
results in a poor growth rate, eczema, and lowered resistance to infectious
diseases.

claims.claim_text: Beyond building protein, several amino acids are the raw material for other key body chemicals, and Wallach lays out the conversions: tryptophan is the precursor of niacin (vitamin B3) and serotonin (the mood neurotransmitter); phenylalanine gives rise to thyroxin (a thyroid hormone) and epinephrine (adrenaline); and methionine is used to form choline and creatine phosphate. It comes from his table of the classic essential amino acids — the ones the body cannot make for itself and must take in from the diet each day.
claims.verbatim:
Tryptophan precursor of niacin and serotonin
Phenylalanine precursor of thyroxin and epinephrine
Methionine formation of choline and creatine phosphate

claims.claim_text: Cholesterol is structural to cell walls and to the brain and spinal cord (myelin), and is the raw material for vitamin D, bile acids, adrenal cortical hormones, estrogen, progesterone, and testosterone.
claims.verbatim:
Cholesterol is an essential part
of the structure of cell walls, brain and spinal cord (myelin), the raw
material for the production of vitamin D in the human body, bile acids,
adrenal cortical hormones, estrogen (a cholesterol deficiency makes
menopause a living hell), progesterone, and testosterone

claims.claim_text: Infertility is usually caused by a nutritional deficiency; Wallach reports curing several hundred cases with supplementation of vitamins, minerals, trace minerals, and digestive aids.
claims.verbatim:
INFERTILITY (curable inability to have children) is usually caused by a
nutritional deficiency of some nutrient. We have “cured” several hundred
cases of infertility by simple supplementation of vitamins, minerals, trace
minerals, and digestive aids.

claims.claim_text: Infertility protocol: EFA 5 g three times daily, L-arginine 500 mg three times daily, zinc, selenium 250 mcg/day, vitamin A 100,000 International Units/day for 30 days then 25,000 International Units/day, and germanium 50 mg/day.
claims.verbatim:
EFA at 5 gm t.i.d., l-arginine at 500 mg t.i.d., zinc at 15 mg t.i.d., selenium
at 250 mcg/day, vitamin A at 100,000 IU/day for 30 days then drop to
25,000 IU/day, germanium at 50 mg/day

claims.claim_text: Selenium prevents muscular dystrophy in all its forms (and Keshan disease, heart muscular dystrophy); preconception selenium levels matter for both pregnancy maintenance and muscular-dystrophy prevention.
claims.verbatim:
The selenium levels in
preconception women is important to the maintenance of pregnancy as well
as the prevention of muscular dystrophy in all of its forms

claims.claim_text: Given selenium and vitamin E (intramuscular [injected into a muscle] or intravenous [into a vein]) at the very first onset of symptoms, muscular dystrophy can be arrested or even cured.
claims.verbatim:
If selenium and vitamin E were to
be given IM or IV at the very first onset of symptoms, the disease will be
arrested or maybe even “cured.”

claims.claim_text: Muscle cramps (charley horse) are a mini-convulsion in the muscle resulting from deficiencies of calcium, magnesium, potassium, selenium, and/or vitamin E.
claims.verbatim:
MUSCLE CRAMPS (Charley horse) are a “mini” convulsion that is taking
place in the muscle as a result of deficiencies of calcium, magnesium

claims.claim_text: Insomnia treatment includes avoiding caffeine and food allergens, calcium (especially plant-derived colloidal), and chromium + vanadium at 25-200 mcg three times daily.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment for insomnia includes avoidance of caffeine and offending food allergens, calcium
(especially plant derived colloidal calcium), chromium and vanadium at 25-200 mcg t.i.d.

claims.claim_text: A lasting loss of the sense of smell — known medically as anosmia — is most often the result of a zinc deficiency, Wallach says. He separates this chronic loss from the temporary kind caused by a cold or nasal inflammation, and notes that zinc supplementation (he uses 50 mg three times a day) is very effective at restoring smell — except where the underlying cause is an injury, stroke, or tumor.
claims.verbatim:
Chronic loss of the sense of
smell is most frequently the result of a zinc deficiency.

claims.claim_text: Anxiety/panic treatment: avoid caffeine and sugar; chromium + vanadium 200-300 mcg/day, B6 100 mg three times daily, B3 450 mg three times daily, L-tryptophan, calcium 2,000 mg/day, magnesium 800 mg/day.
claims.verbatim:
Take chromium and vanadium
200-300 mcg/day, B6 100 mg t.i.d., B3 450 mg t.i.d. as time-release tablets,
B1, B2, and B5 at the rate of 50 mg t.i.d., L-tryptophan 10 grams t.i.d.,
calcium 2000 mg/day, and magnesium at 800 mg/day.

claims.claim_text: Wallach ties poor appetite to mineral status, not just psychology: deficiencies of the minerals zinc and lithium are associated with anorexia (loss of appetite). In the same discussion he goes further, arguing that anorexia nervosa — usually treated as a psychiatric disease — is often a manifestation of a severe food allergy, since sufferers commonly feel better when they don't eat. His answer is to correct the deficiency, hunt down the offending food (frequently cow's milk, wheat, eggs, or corn), and support digestion with betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes alongside the baseline vitamin-mineral program.
claims.verbatim: Deficiencies of zinc and lithium are associated with anorexia.

claims.claim_text: Canker sores (aphthous stomatitis): folic acid 5 mg three times daily, B12 1,000 mcg/day, iron 15 mg/day, and zinc 50 mg three times daily as adjuncts to allergen-avoidance diets.
claims.verbatim:
Folic acid at 5 mg ti.d., B12 at 1000 mcg/day, iron at 15 mg/day and zinc at
50 mg t.i.d. are effective adjuncts to avoidance diets.

claims.claim_text: For arsenic toxicity, intravenous (into a vein) chelation and oral colloidal/chelated selenium effectively remove the body's arsenic load.
claims.verbatim:
IV chelation is very effective in removing
the body load of arsenic, as is the oral use of colloidal or chelated selenium.

claims.claim_text: This is one of Wallach's signature cardiovascular claims: magnesium deficiency, he says, produces a 'malignant calcification' of the elastic arteries — the aorta and other large vessels — and may be nothing less than 'the cause' of arteriosclerosis, the hardening of the arteries. In his framing the calcium hardening the artery wall is a downstream sign of a missing mineral, magnesium, rather than the primary villain — a direct challenge to the conventional cholesterol-centered story of heart disease.
claims.verbatim:
Magnesium deficiencies produce “malignant calcification” of
elastic arteries and are perhaps “the cause” of arteriosclerosis.

claims.claim_text: Vitamin D toxicity (angiotoxicity) targets the elastic arteries, causing fibrosis of the vascular smooth muscle and calcification of the vessel wall.
claims.verbatim:
The target tissue of vitamin D toxicity is the
elastic arteries and the specific result is fibrosis of the vascular smooth
muscle and calcification of the blood vessel wall

claims.claim_text: Age-related prostate enlargement (benign prostatic hyperplasia) is usually the result of a zinc deficiency.
claims.verbatim:
As the prostate
enlarges with age (usually the result of a zinc deficiency)

claims.claim_text: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (enlarged prostate) treatment: zinc 50 mg three times daily, flaxseed-oil EFAs 9 g/day, high-fiber diet with pumpkin seeds, 300,000 International Units vitamin A as beta-carotene/day, and selenium 250 mcg three times daily.
claims.verbatim:
Benign prostatic hypertrophy is treated with zinc at 50 mg t.i.d., essential
fatty acids as flaxseed oil at 9 grams per day, high fiber diets including
pumpkin seeds and alfalfa, 300,000 IU vitamin A as beta carotene per day,
vitamin C to bowel tolerance, chlorophyll (best source is alfalfa), amino
acids (glycine, alanine, and glutamic acid) at five grams each daily for 90
days, hydrogen peroxide (20 drops per oz. of aloe juice) at 1 oz. b.i.d.,
unsweetened cranberry juice at two pints per day, herbs including saw
palmetto (Serenoa serrulata), and selenium at 250 mcg t.i.d.

claims.claim_text: Bell's palsy treatment: B12 1,000 mcg/day to a total of 20,000 mcg, calcium/magnesium 2,000 and 800 mg/day, and essential fatty acids 5 g three times daily.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment is B12 at 1000 mcg/day for a total of 20,000 mcg, calcium/
magnesium at 2,000 mg and 800 mg per day, essential fatty acids at 5 gm
t.i.d.

claims.claim_text: Kidney/bladder stones are ironically caused by a calcium- and/or magnesium-deficient diet — the stone minerals come from your own bones.
claims.verbatim:
BLADDER STONES (kidney stones, cystic calculi) are ironically caused
by a calcium and/or a magnesium deficient diet

claims.claim_text: Wallach teaches that bladder and kidney stones are, ironically, caused by a calcium- and/or magnesium-deficient diet together with raging osteoporosis — the minerals that form the stones are pulled from your own bones. Prevention therefore means correcting that deficiency rather than avoiding calcium: he calls calcium at 2,000 mg and magnesium at 1,000 mg daily imperative to stop the calcium loss from the bones, and adds reducing meat intake (shifting toward the vegetarian scale) to bring the dietary calcium-to-phosphorus ratio back in order.
claims.verbatim:
BLADDER STONES (kidney stones, cystic calculi) are ironically caused
by a calcium and/or a magnesium deficient diet and when you
have raging osteoporosis. The minerals in the
“stones” come from your own bones!!! Diagnosis may require an x-ray (a
flat “plate” of the abdomen). Don’t forget the gonadal shield!!! The signal
to think “stones” is blood in the urine (use the urine test sticks) and pain or
“colic” that gets worse in the bladder or kidney area. “Stones” are
potentially very painful and may require Tylenol-3 or morphine to cope
with the pain if they are obstructing a ureter (the tube from the kidney to the
bladder).
Treatment should include an anti-inflammatory medication such as licorice
(Glycyrrhiza glabra) to reduce swelling at the “log jam” so the “stones” can
pass. If this isn’t strong enough, you may have to resort to prednisone for
three (3) days to accomplish this part of the therapy. Calcium and
magnesium at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg is imperative to stop calcium loss

claims.claim_text: Easy bleeding or bruising under the skin can be a nutritional clue, Wallach notes: it may point to a vitamin E or vitamin K deficiency — both vitamins tied to normal blood clotting — or to an overdose of prescription blood thinners. He is careful to separate this from bleeding in the stool, which he warns is a different and potentially serious sign that calls for real diagnostic follow-up.
claims.verbatim:
Bleeding under the skin may indicate vitamin E or vitamin K
deficiencies

claims.claim_text: In a normal gradual menopause, the adrenals and liver increase female-hormone (estrogen) output to make up for lost ovarian function; insufficient output produces hot flashes and night sweats.
claims.verbatim:
the adrenals and liver increase their
output of female hormones (primarily estrogen) and make up the difference
from the lost ovarian function.

claims.claim_text: On menopause, Wallach's stance is that estrogen supplements should not be used, because they raise the risk of inducing breast and uterine cancer. He treats menopause not as a disease needing hormone 'treatment' but as a normal transition to support: as the ovaries wind down, the adrenals and liver take over female-hormone production, and the aim is to smooth that shift — with the base-line supplement program plus extra calcium and magnesium, two eggs and red meat daily, a monthly liver flush, betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes, and herbs such as lady's mantle, motherwort and St. John's wort.
claims.verbatim:
Estrogen supplements should not be used as
they increase the breast and uterine cancer induction risk.

claims.claim_text: For menopause — which Wallach frames as a normal transition needing 'support,' not a disease to 'treat' — his plan pairs the baseline supplement program with calcium at 2,000 mg and magnesium at 1,000 mg a day, plus traditional women's herbs such as lady's mantle, motherwort, and St. John's wort. He pointedly avoids estrogen supplements, arguing they raise the risk of breast and uterine cancer, and leans on nutrition to smooth the change and head off the osteoporosis that can follow.
claims.verbatim:
Use the base line supplement program, plus calcium and magnesium
at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day

claims.claim_text: Wallach's explanation for why there is still no cold vaccine is simple: the common cold (nasal catarrh, or coryza) isn't one illness but the work of more than 100 different viruses, so no single shot can cover them all. He notes colds run a self-limited 7 to 14 days regardless of treatment, arrive fast after a short 1-to-3-day incubation, and are best met with heavy vitamin C rather than antibiotics, which do nothing against a virus.
claims.verbatim:
COLDS (nasal catarrh, coryza) are caused by more than 100 different
viruses, this is why no vaccine has been made available.

claims.claim_text: Common-cold treatment: vitamin C to bowel tolerance, bioflavonoids 150 mg three times daily, garlic, the baseline supplement program, and chicken-rice soup.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of the “common cold” should include vitamin C to bowel
tolerance, bioflavonoids at 150 mg t.i.d., garlic, gelatin capsules t.i.d.

claims.claim_text: Wallach identifies salt (sodium chloride) as the raw material the stomach needs to manufacture its acid, so people on salt-restricted diets are more prone to achlorhydria (loss of stomach acid). Achlorhydria brings 'burp, belch, and bloat,' lets intestinal bacteria and yeast ferment high-carbohydrate foods in the stomach, and leads to B12, calcium, and protein deficiencies plus new adult-onset food allergies from absorbing partly digested proteins -- so his treatment starts with putting salt back on your food.
claims.verbatim:
Sodium chloride is the
raw material required to manufacture stomach acid, so it follows that people
on a salt restricted diet are more likely to
develop achlorhydria.
Symptoms include “burp, belch, and bloat” after eating. The reduction or
absence of acid in the stomach allows intestinal bacteria and yeast (Candida
albicans) to enter the stomach and ferment high carbohydrate foods (i.e.
juice, fruit, breads, etc.). Failure to deal with achlorhydria will result in
B12, calcium, and protein deficiencies and the onset of new food allergies
acquired later in life as a result of absorption of partially digested
polypeptides (relatively large protein fragments) which trigger an allergic
response.
Treatment of achlorhydria includes salting your food to taste and
supplementation of betaine HCl at the rate of 75-250 mg 15-20 minutes
before each meal.

claims.claim_text: Wallach warns that a diet high in vegetable oils (salad dressing, cooking oils) combined with low selenium is the fastest path to heart attack and cancer, because heating or hydrogenating the polyunsaturated oils turns them into trans fats and rancid, "free radical"-damaged cellular fat.
claims.verbatim:
High intakes of vegetable oils,
including salad dressing and cooking oils, concurrent with a selenium
deficiency is the quickest route to a heart attack and cancer.

claims.claim_text: Wallach teaches that age spots (liver spots) are rancid fat — ceroid lipofuscin or trans fatty acids — from cell walls accumulating under the skin; ten on the back of the hand mean millions in the organs, and they flag a high risk of cancer and heart disease. Because they are reversible, his treatment is to eliminate all fried foods and vegetable oils (salad dressing, cooking oils, margarine) plus sugar, with selenium and vitamin E.
claims.verbatim:
These unsightly brown
spots are caused by rancid fat (ceroid lipofuscin or trans fatty acids)from
cell walls accumulating under the skin. If you have ten on the back of your
hand, you have millions in your brain, heart, liver, kidney, lungs, etc. They
interfere with cell function, shorten your life, and are a red flag warning for
high risk of cancer and heart disease (i.e. cardiomyopathy). The nice thing
about age spots is that they are reversible. When they go away on the
outside, they are going away on the inside.
Treatment includes eliminating all fried foods, vegetable oils (i.e. salad
dressing, cooking oils, margarine, etc.), and sugar from the diet.

claims.claim_text: For Alzheimer's, Wallach says to replace the cholesterol the brain needs to rebuild myelin by eating soft-scrambled (not fried) eggs every day plus 72 oz of red meat each month.
claims.verbatim:
500 mcg
selenium daily and IV chelation will be of value. Eat soft-scrambled (not
fried) eggs every day and 72 oz. red meat each month to replace cholesterol
needed to rebuild myelin.

claims.claim_text: Wallach warns that fried eggs trigger 93 percent of all gallbladder attacks (with fried onions, fried potatoes and pork close behind) -- a reason to poach, boil or soft-scramble eggs rather than fry them.
claims.verbatim:
the base line
nutritional supplement including 5 gm of EFA t.i.d. Fried eggs are known to
precipitate 93 percent of all gallbladder attacks, followed closely by fried
onions, fried potatoes, and pork.

claims.claim_text: For the early stage of treating diabetes, Wallach says to cut all natural and processed sugar and refined carbs and instead eat meat, eggs and poultry three to six times a day to stabilize blood sugar.
claims.verbatim:
No natural
or processed sugar and carbohydrates should be consumed. Eat meat, eggs,
and poultry three to six times per day to stabilize blood sugar in the
beginning stages of the therapy.

claims.claim_text: For MS and ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease), Wallach says avoiding fried foods and margarine (plus taking fish or flax oil) raises survival, and that eating the cholesterol in eggs and red meat is critically important because the myelin sheath is made almost entirely of cholesterol.
claims.verbatim:
It is known that avoidance of fried foods and margarine
and a relatively high consumption of flaxseed oil or fish oil (cod liver oil or
salmon oil) at 5 gm t.i.d. will increase your survival rate by 50 percent. The
consumption of cholesterol (eggs and red meat) is of extreme importance as
the myelin sheath that disappears in MS is made almost exclusively of
cholesterol.

claims.claim_text: For an underactive thyroid, Wallach's first dietary step is to cut out goitrogenic foods — including cruciferous vegetables like cabbage — before adding thyroid support.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of hypothyroidism includes eliminating all goiterogenic
substances such as nitrates, cabbage, etc. Supplement with U.S. Armour
thyroid at 1 to 3 grains each morning.

claims.claim_text: For everyday drinking Wallach recommends filtered water over distilled: distilled water is 'hungry' water, and used long-term it leaches minerals out of your bones, thinning them.
claims.verbatim:
drink filtered —not distilled—water. Distilled water
is “hungry” water and will demineralize your bones over a long period of
usage.

claims.claim_text: Wallach warns against carbonated soft drinks: every one of them is loaded with phosphates, and over the long haul those phosphates drive osteoporosis - a special concern for anyone already on a restricted diet.
claims.verbatim:
avoid carbonated soft drinks which ALL are loaded with phosphates which
will cause osteoporosis over the long haul especially when you are already
on a restricted diet

claims.claim_text: Yes — emphatically. In Wallach's account of the Hunza, the people he describes as relatively disease-free and living well past a hundred, butter is a staple rather than an afterthought: they put it in their tea and use it as a cooking shortening, and it sits among their core fat sources alongside whole milk, ghee, apricot oil and animal fats. He lists those fat sources as one of the 14 Hunza practices that contribute to their longevity.
claims.verbatim: Fat sources include whole milk, butter, ghee, apricot oil, and animal fats.

claims.claim_text: For menopause, Wallach's protocol has the person eat red meat once each day, plus 2 eggs daily and a monthly liver flush, on top of the base-line supplement program with calcium and magnesium.
claims.verbatim:
Eat two eggs
every day, red meat once each day, and the liver flush at least once per
month. Use the base line supplement program, plus calcium and magnesium
at 2,000 mg and 1,000 mg per day

claims.claim_text: Wallach tells some people to cut back on red meat because it is heavy in phosphorus relative to calcium; for phosphorus-driven bone conditions like Paget's disease he says to reduce or eliminate red meat to correct the calcium/phosphorus ratio.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of Paget’s Disease should include a vigorous effort to correct the
dietary calcium/phosphorus ratio, reduce or eliminate red meat intake, avoid
phosphate containing soft drinks, avoid all phosphate containing
supplements

claims.claim_text: Wallach credits the longer average lifespan of Mormons and Seventh-Day Adventists partly to their avoidance of fried foods, and he lists fried pork first among the fried foods to skip.
claims.verbatim:
Mormons and Seventh Day Adventists live to be 82
years of age on the average because they avoid caffeine (i.e. coffee, soft
drinks, tea, iced tea, etc.), alcohol, smoking, and fried foods (i.e. pork,
catfish, shrimp, lard shortening, etc).

claims.claim_text: Whole egg tops Wallach's protein-quality chart with a chemical score of 100 and 94% utilization, higher than human milk, cow's milk, or soybean, making it his benchmark for usable protein.
claims.verbatim:
The availability and usability of N from various foods are
quite different and must be considered when choosing N sources.
Nitrogen/Protein Utilization Values of Common Foods
Nitrogen Source (Protein) Chemical Score % Utilization
Whole egg 100 94
Human milk 100 87
Cow’s milk 95 82
Soy bean 74 65

claims.claim_text: Yes, but only a trace — and it is not a reason to eat tuna. Germanium is a trace element Wallach prizes as an immune booster (it stimulates natural killer cells, interferon, macrophages and T-suppressor cells) and an oxygen-utilization cofactor, with deficiency typified by a severely reduced immune status, arthritis, osteoporosis, low energy and cancer. But tuna carries only about 2.3 ppm of germanium — actually less than ordinary beans at 4.67 ppm, and far below the germanium-rich healing herbs and foods like garlic, ginseng and shiitake mushrooms (100 to 2,000 ppm). So fish is a minor incidental source at best — not a meaningful way to get germanium.
claims.verbatim:
Food plants and animals contain small amounts of germanium (i.e. beans—
4.67 ppm, tuna—2.3 ppm).

claims.claim_text: Essential fatty acids are required every day at 3% of total daily calorie intake, or 9 g per day when supplemented in capsule form. The 9 g is one combined amount for the essential fatty acids together, not 9 g of each.
claims.verbatim:
Essential fatty acids are a
must and should be consumed at the rate of 3 percent of your total daily
calorie consumption or supplemented at the rate of 9 grams per day in
capsule form.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's origin story for plant-derived colloidal minerals. He credits a specific product — Mineral Toddy, made by a company called Rockland U.S.A. — that he came across at Hospital Santa Monica. What made it work, he says, was where it came from: a prehistoric deposit of buried plant matter that had never turned into oil, coal, or stone. That escape from geological compression is why the minerals in it were still in the form the original plants had made them, ready for the body to use, rather than trapped back inside rock.
claims.verbatim:
Mineral Toddy was produced by Rockland U.S.A. from a unique prehistoric
plant deposit that had never been compressed into oil or coal. It had never
been fossilized or petrified.

claims.claim_text: Two claims about the same liquid, side by side. First: it carries 77 different minerals — more than the 60 Wallach counts as essential to a human body, so a single bottle covers the full essential spectrum and then some. Second: up to 98% of what you swallow is 'bio-available,' meaning the body can actually absorb and use it rather than pass it straight through. Both, in his framing, follow from the same fact: these minerals were built by living plants, not milled out of rock. A mineral's usefulness, to him, depends on which of those two things made it.
claims.verbatim:
The value of this tea colored liquid was that it
contained 77 minerals in the plant derived colloidal form. Because they
were plant derived colloidal minerals instead of from ground up rocks, they
were up to 98 percent bio-available.

claims.claim_text: The single step at the heart of Wallach's whole mineral framework — and the reason he cares about the source. Rock ground into fine dust and suspended in water is real minerals, but in a form that living cells can't take in. Plants can. Their roots pull those rock minerals up from the soil and rebuild them inside their own cells into a different chemical form — the form every living cell of every plant, animal, and human is actually built out of. So a mineral in a rock and the same mineral in a piece of broccoli, he argues, are not the same nutrient. A plant is the factory that does the one step your body can't do for itself, which is why he says the source matters.
claims.verbatim:
Plants, including wild forms and crops such as grains, vegetables, fruits,
and nuts, take up these inorganic metallic colloids and convert them into
intracellular (within the cell) organically bound plant colloids. These
organic plant colloids are the form of minerals found in and used by all
living cells of plants, animals, and humans.

claims.claim_text: 'Age Beaters' is Wallach's shorthand for the eight unrelated long-lived cultures he tracks — populations where reaching 100+ in good health is common rather than exceptional. What ties them together, he argues, is what grows in their fields: each settled by chance in a high arid valley below a glacier and built canals to bring the glacier's mineral-rich meltwater ('glacial milk') to their crops, which converted those inorganic minerals into plant-derived colloidal form. Those plant-derived colloidal minerals in their food, he says, are the common thread behind the shared longevity — and why he calls them, flatly, the Fountain of Youth.
claims.verbatim:
It is the plant derived colloidal minerals in their grains,
vegetables, fruits, and nuts that are their common threads giving the Age Beaters their health and longevity. It is the plant derived colloidal
minerals that are in fact the Fountain of Youth!

claims.claim_text: Wallach's own honest limit on Mineral Toddy, stated a few sentences after listing what it fixed. The colloidal liquid, he says, carries every mineral only in trace amounts. That is enough for the trace minerals the body needs in tiny amounts, but to even come close to the mainstream Recommended Daily Allowances it has to be paired with a separate source of what he calls the "major minerals and electrolytes": calcium, magnesium, manganese, zinc, and potassium. In the same passage he put the minerals in calcium-enriched orange juice, which both masked their harsh astringent taste and provided a significant amount of additional calcium — one of those lacking majors. On his own account the colloidal minerals were never meant as a stand-alone mineral supplement — a piece of the picture, not the whole picture.
claims.verbatim:
The colloidal
minerals were all present in trace amounts. They required an additional
source of the major minerals and electrolytes such as calcium, magnesium,
manganese, zinc, and potassium to even come close to the published RDAs.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's punchline to the entire search for longevity. For all of recorded history people have poured out resources, money, and even their lives chasing a Fountain of Youth — and his answer is almost anticlimactic: it was under our feet the whole time. The Fountain of Youth is minerals.
claims.verbatim:
The search for health and longevity is as old as man himself. We have
expended resources, money, energy, and have in fact died in droves looking
for the Fountain of Youth. Literally the Fountain of Youth has been under
our feet since the beginning of time. The answer is almost anticlimactic; it’s
minerals.

claims.claim_text: What the raw liquid actually tastes like. Plant-derived colloidal minerals are intensely astringent — Wallach says that taken straight, undiluted, they would 'shrink wrap your lips over your teeth.' That is why they are taken stirred into juice rather than drunk on their own.
claims.verbatim:
The plant derived colloidal minerals were very astringent. Taken “straight,”
they’d “shrink wrap your lips over your teeth” if you drank
them without juice.

claims.claim_text: How Wallach came to colloidal minerals. He had never even heard of them until he encountered the liquid being served to patients at Hospital Santa Monica. Excited by the new tool, he gathered every book and article ever written on colloids, and within three months had absorbed essentially everything then known about them.
claims.verbatim:
I got excited about this new-found nutritional tool, and I gathered every
piece of information that I could find on plant derived colloidal minerals. I
had never heard of colloidal minerals until this moment in my professional
career so I began to educate myself. I gathered every book and every article
that had ever been written on colloidal minerals and within three months I
was familiar with just about everything historically and currently known
about colloids and plant derived colloidal minerals.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's own account of the fight to keep plant-derived colloidal minerals high-quality — and a hard lesson about companies that cut corners. The minerals he built his products on came from one particular prehistoric deposit. When the company then bottling them, Eagle, quietly switched to a cheaper source to save about a dollar a gallon, the liquid changed batch to batch: one day thin and tasteless with its astringency gone, the next black like India ink, the next green. Every product built on those minerals suffered, and customers began complaining that 'the minerals didn't work anymore.' When Wallach objected, Eagle denied anything had changed, and in early 1997 terminated his distributorship, wanting a quieter corporate image. Rather than accept a degraded product, Wallach founded his own company, American Longevity, and went straight back to Elmer Heinrich of Rockland — the original deposit the minerals had come from since 1991 — relaunching them as 'Virgin Earth' plant-derived colloidal minerals. He went back to the proven source. The lasting lesson for anyone buying these minerals: the source deposit is what makes them work, and a cheaper source is not the same product.
claims.verbatim:
The Mineral Toddy, however, was beginning to change. One day you could
drink a quart of Toddy minerals like water because the astringent character
of the minerals was gone. The next batch of Mineral Toddy was black like
India Ink. The next batch was green. The obvious changes in the Mineral
Toddy negatively affected all of the products that used the minerals as a
base.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's opening thesis, framed as science. He treats the world's long-lived cultures as a living 'control group' — five ancient, very different peoples who all reached healthful, disease-free longevity, with steady access to all ninety essential nutrients the body needs. The secret they shared, he says, was unique natural sources of plant-derived colloidal minerals, and his promise is that anyone who taps that same accumulated knowledge can do the same.
claims.verbatim:
This control group of five
ancient and highly diverse cultures share common denominators that
include healthful, disease-free longevity, and unlimited access to adequate
levels of all ninety essential nutrients required by humans. One of the
secrets they shared includes access to unique natural sources of plant
derived colloidal minerals. My promise to you is that if you plug into the
thousands of years of accumulated knowledge of these long-lived peoples,
you and yours can make it too!

claims.claim_text: Microplastics are a modern problem Wallach's books never take up. But they fall squarely into a category he does address: xenobiotics — the foreign compounds the body has to recognize and clear. In a selenium review he quotes approvingly across several books, the mineral is described as 'involved in detoxification of metals and certain xenobiotics,' one of the body's built-in tools for handling foreign chemicals. From there his general defense against toxin load is consistent: keep selenium up (he runs 250 to 500 mcg a day in his prevention programs), lean on plant-derived colloidal minerals to 'reduce your risk of damage from heavy metals and pollution,' filter your home's water and air, and run a periodic detox. None of this is Wallach speaking about plastics specifically — it is his framework for foreign-chemical exposure, which microplastics now fall under.
claims.verbatim:
selenium acts as an acceptor of
biogenic methyl groups, and is involved in detoxification of metals and
certain xenobiotics. Selenium also has immunopotentiating properties.

claims.claim_text: As part of his cancer-prevention program, Wallach lays out a simple ongoing detox routine: take alfalfa daily 'in some form as a detoxifier,' do a liver flush once or twice a month by drinking apple juice for three days, and get a hair analysis each year — which he uses both to monitor toxic-metal load and to check how well you're absorbing minerals (if absorption is poor, he notes, all your mineral levels run low). It sits inside a broader daily regimen for keeping toxins down: dietary fiber at every meal, filtered (not distilled) water, 2 to 3 bowel movements a day, biodegradable household cleaners, and organic food wherever possible. The hair analysis is the feedback loop — it is how he would tell whether the metals are actually coming down.
claims.verbatim:
Take alfalfa daily in some form
as a detoxifier. Do a liver flush once or twice each month by drinking apple
juice for three days. Do a hair analysis each year to monitor toxic metal
load as well as absorption capability.

claims.claim_text: Achlorhydria — what causes it, and how common it is. Achlorhydria means the loss of the stomach's hydrochloric acid (HCl). Wallach names two causes, and says both run opposite to what most people assume. The first is stress — contrary to popular belief it does not raise stomach acid, it shuts acid production down, and he pins the moment: once stress passes the point of decompensation, where the body can no longer compensate. The second is age itself, a natural process he calls perhaps the most significant aging phenomenon, at 75 percent of people over 50 requiring supplemental stomach acid. A third contributor is dietary: ordinary salt (sodium chloride) is the raw material the stomach uses to manufacture its acid, so people on salt-restricted diets are more likely to become achlorhydric. The everyday sign is 'burp, belch, and bloat' after eating.
claims.verbatim:
ACHLORHYDRIA (loss of stomach acid—hydrochloric acid): Contrary
to popular belief, stress will result in loss of stomach acid production.
Achlorhydria is also a natural process of aging and perhaps the most
significant aging phenomenon. Seventy-five percent of people over the age
of 50 years require supplementation of stomach acid.

claims.claim_text: Chronic dyspepsia — what it costs if you leave it. Dyspepsia means poor digestion, and Wallach describes it by its everyday signs: belching, burping, bloating and 'acid stomach.' His explanation inverts the usual one — the trouble is not too much acid but that the stomach's acid is not acid enough, so food ferments and the gas is burped back up. He calls it probably the most common 'disease' in the western world and certainly the most costly, measured by what people spend on relief — but says the real cost is what it becomes: food allergies, osteoporosis, anemia, a debilitated immune system, degenerative disease. Prevention is reduced stress, exercise, healthful diet habits and reasonable food volumes; and because stomach-acid production falls as we age — an unforgiving event, and the main cause of dyspepsia in seniors — the regular use of digestive aids.
claims.verbatim:
Dyspepsia is probably the most common
“disease” in the western world and is certainly the most costly from the
amount of money spent on “relief.” Even more costly is the secondary
results of chronic dyspepsia: food allergies, osteoporosis, anemia,
debilitated immune system, degenerative disease. Prevention includes
reduced stress levels, exercise, healthful diet habits, and reasonable food
volumes. An unforgiving event as we age is a decrease in stomach acid
production, the main cause of dyspepsia in seniors. Prevention in this case
includes the regular use of digestive aids.

claims.claim_text: Antacids versus digestive aids. Wallach's position on antacids is split, and the split follows from his account of indigestion. In an emergency they are a good temporary fix. As a regular habit they harm you — regular use will eventually damage you by reducing the nutrients you absorb — because the stomach's acid is already not acid enough, so neutralizing it further undercuts the digestion and absorption that acid exists to drive. What he prescribes instead is replacement rather than suppression: 75 to 200 mg of betaine hydrochloride (a supplemental form of stomach acid) with pancreatic enzymes, three times a day, 15 to 30 minutes before each meal. His herbal preventions and remedies are papaya, common barberry, and bitters such as gentian — and in some cases a glass of wine or several ounces of vinegar before meals will help.
claims.verbatim:
Treatment of dyspepsia includes supplementation of 75-200 mg betaine
HCl and pancreatic enzymes t.i.d. 15-30 minutes before each meal.
“Antacids” are a good “temporary fix” in an emergency, but regular use will
eventually damage you by reducing the nutrients you absorb.

claims.claim_text: Who should take digestive aids, and why. Wallach gives this instruction as part of preventing candidiasis — the Candida albicans overgrowth he ties to chronic fatigue syndrome — and the reasoning is what makes the advice land. Candida is a normally harmless yeast living on the skin, mouth, vagina and intestine. It turns pathological when the gut's competing normal bacteria are killed off by long-term antibiotic use, or when low stomach acid (hypochlorhydria, usually the result of salt restriction) lets it move up into the stomach — a location it does not normally occupy. Stress reduces stomach acid once it reaches the point of decompensation, and food allergies change the lining of the gut in a way very similar to celiac disease, raising the nutrient concentration in the gut into a 'hyperfertilized' environment the yeast finds attractive; eventually the overgrowth spills into the bloodstream. So his prevention starts with knowing your own digestive and absorptive patterns: pulse-test for food allergies, avoid long-term antibiotics, and as you grow older take betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals to offset the normal decrease in stomach-acid production. He is emphatic on two more points — take these digestive aids if you are under stress, and deal aggressively with any disease that lowers your immune capacity.
claims.verbatim:
Prevention includes being aware of your intestines and knowing your
digestive and absorptive abilities and patterns. Do pulse tests for food
allergies, avoid long term use of antibiotics, and as you grow older take
betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals to offset the normal
decrease in production of stomach acid. Be sure to take these digestive aids
if you are under stress; deal aggressively with any disease that lowers your
immune capacity!

claims.claim_text: Gastric bloating — where the gas actually comes from. Bloating is the accumulation of gas in the stomach, and Wallach's explanation turns on a fact most people don't know: a healthy stomach is sterile, and it stays that way because it is so acidic. When hypochlorhydria — low stomach acid — sets in, that sterility fails, and bacteria and yeast from the small intestine migrate upward into the stomach, a place they do not belong. There they ferment the carbohydrates and sugars you have eaten, and the gas that fermentation produces is the 'bloat.' It is the same picture he draws for achlorhydria, where the symptom triad is 'burp, belch, and bloat,' and it explains why his treatment goes after the missing acid — colloidal minerals, betaine HCl and pancreatic enzymes before meals — rather than after the gas.
claims.verbatim:
BLOATING (gastric) is the accumulation of gas in the stomach. Normally
the stomach is sterile because of the acid environment; however, when
hypochlorhydria (low stomach acid) occurs, bacteria and yeast from the
small intestine migrates up into the stomach. The bacteria in the stomach
now “ferments” carbohydrates and sugars that are eaten and produce gas or
“bloat.”

claims.claim_text: Dumping syndrome — why an acid intestine disables your enzymes. Dumping syndrome is the sudden emptying of stomach contents into the small intestine all at once, overloading the intestine's natural buffer system. That matters because of where the body's acid is meant to sit: the stomach is supposed to be strongly acidic, the small intestine is not, and pancreatic enzymes require an alkaline environment to function — so when unbuffered acid floods in, they stop working properly. Wallach notes it is a common side effect of stomach surgery, and that anemia and osteoporosis are its common secondary diseases, which is what you would expect from a stretch of gut that can no longer digest and absorb.
